Well, anxious? I don't know if anxious is exactly the right word for it, though I guess it kind of feels like that sometimes. It's more like... okay, so when I pull up one of those spreadsheets, right? The weekly summary one. I'll open it up, and almost immediately I get this sort of... heavy, restless feeling in my chest. Not like a panic attack or anything—my wife had one of those once, and it's definitely not that—but just this immense dread. Because I know I have to sit there for the next hour and just stare at these tiny little cells on the screen. 

And then, as I'm doing it, I'm constantly second-guessing myself. Like, I'll type in a number, say, 4,500, and my brain will immediately go, 'Wait, was that 4,500 or 5,400?' So I have to look back at the dashboard, verify it, look back at the spreadsheet, and by the time I've done that three times for one single cell, I'm just... I'm so tense. My shoulders are practically up to my ears. I actually had to buy a different desk chair because my neck was hurting so bad from how tense I get. 

But is it stress from the work itself? Not really. I mean, the math isn't hard. It's literally just data transfer. It's the stress of knowing that I'm probably going to mess it up, no matter how hard I try. It's like walking on eggshells in my own brain. And with the checklists, it's the same thing. I'll be going down the line—check, check, check—and I'll start feeling this pressure, like I need to get it done faster, even if there's no real deadline. I just want to be done with it so badly that I end up rushing, and then I get stressed because I know rushing is exactly how I miss a line, but I can't seem to make myself just slow down and look at it calmly. It's just this constant, exhausting tug-of-war in my head the entire time I'm doing these tasks.

A racing heart or sweating? No, no, definitely not trembling. It's driving me absolutely crazy. \n\nLike, I'll be looking right at our team dashboard, which is where all the guys' daily numbers get pooled, and I have to transfer that data into the weekly summary for upper management. And I will literally copy the completely wrong numbers. I'll look right at the screen and type something else, or pull from the wrong column entirely. Or, like, we have these procedural checklists I'm supposed to review for the reps to make sure they're hitting compliance, and I'll just completely miss a line. Just skip right over it without even realizing it. \n\nAnd the most frustrating part—the part that really gets to me and makes me feel like I'm losing my mind—is that I always check my work. I'll sit there, I'll read through the whole report, I'll think I went over it perfectly and everything is good to go, and then my manager will ping me an hour later asking where on earth I got a certain figure. It makes me look so careless, but I'm really trying, I just... I don't know how I keep missing these details when I'm staring right at them.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself making similar mistakes outside of work, like in your personal life or hobbies?\n\nPatient: You know, it's funny you ask that, because I've actually thought about that a lot lately. You'd think if I was doing it at work, I'd be doing it at home, right? But... honestly, no. Not really. I mean, I've really racked my brain trying to think if I do this kind of thing with, like, paying bills or reading instructions for something around the house. I actually just put together this massive gas grill over the weekend—one of those ones with, like, a hundred different screws and washers and ten different grates—and I followed the manual perfectly. Didn't miss a single step, didn't have any extra pieces left over, which is always the fear, right? \n\nAnd with my hobbies... I restore old motorcycles. Just as a weekend thing, you know? It's something my dad got me into when I was in high school. And when I'm in the garage working on an engine, I am locked in. I mean, you can't afford to make careless mistakes when you're rebuilding a carburetor. If you miss a tiny little jet or put a gasket on backwards, the whole thing runs like garbage, or it doesn't run at all. But I never mess that stuff up. I can sit there for three hours meticulously cleaning and organizing every single tiny part, and I don't miss a thing. \n\nSo it's really just... it's just the work stuff. It's the spreadsheets and the checklists and the data entry. When I'm doing that, my brain just sort of... slips, I guess? But at home, or when I'm doing something I actually care about or that's hands-on, I don't have that problem at all. Which almost makes it worse, you know? Because my manager probably thinks I just don't care about the job, but I do! I really do. It's just... I don't know why it only happens there.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or stressed when you're working on these sales reports or checking procedural checklists?\n\nPatient: Well, anxious? I don't know if anxious is exactly the right word for it, though I guess it kind of feels like that sometimes. It's more like... okay, so when I pull up one of those spreadsheets, right? The weekly summary one. I'll open it up, and almost immediately I get this sort of... heavy, restless feeling in my chest. Not like a panic attack or anything—my wife had one of those once, and it's definitely not that—but just this immense dread. Because I know I have to sit there for the next hour and just stare at these tiny little cells on the screen. \n\nAnd then, as I'm doing it, I'm constantly second-guessing myself. Like, I'll type in a number, say, 4,500, and my brain will immediately go, 'Wait, was that 4,500 or 5,400?' So I have to look back at the dashboard, verify it, look back at the spreadsheet, and by the time I've done that three times for one single cell, I'm just... I'm so tense. My shoulders are practically up to my ears. I actually had to buy a different desk chair because my neck was hurting so bad from how tense I get. \n\nBut is it stress from the work itself? Not really. I mean, the math isn't hard. It's literally just data transfer. It's the stress of knowing that I'm probably going to mess it up, no matter how hard I try. It's like walking on eggshells in my own brain. And with the checklists, it's the same thing. I'll be going down the line—check, check, check—and I'll start feeling this pressure, like I need to get it done faster, even if there's no real deadline. I just want to be done with it so badly that I end up rushing, and then I get stressed because I know rushing is exactly how I miss a line, but I can't seem to make myself just slow down and look at it calmly. It's just this constant, exhausting tug-of-war in my head the entire time I'm doing these tasks.\n\nDoctor: Are you experiencing any difficulties with memory or attention in your personal relationships?\n\nPatient: Yeah, actually, I do. But then I leave work, I drive my normal route, I get home, walk through the door, and he's standing there waiting for it... and my stomach just drops because I completely forgot. It just vanished from my brain the second I left the office parking lot. And it's not just a one-time thing, I forget to pick up something I told my kids I'd bring all the time. They get so disappointed, and my wife gets frustrated because she feels like she has to manage everything or else it falls through the cracks.\n\nAnd she's kind of right, because it happens with household stuff, too. I just keep dropping the ball on all these everyday things, and it makes the people in my life think I'm ignoring them or that I don't care, which isn't true at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself avoiding your work tasks or putting them off because of the frustration or anxiety they cause you?\n\nPatient: Well, avoid them? Disconnected? Detached? Hmm... I'm trying to think if that's the right word for it. I mean, I definitely zone out, right? I don't know why it only happens there.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or stressed when you're working on these sales reports or checking procedural checklists?\n\nPatient: Well, anxious? I don't know if anxious is exactly the right word for it, though I guess it kind of feels like that sometimes. It's more like... okay, so when I pull up one of those spreadsheets, right? The weekly summary one. I'll open it up, and almost immediately I get this sort of... heavy, restless feeling in my chest. Not like a panic attack or anything—my wife had one of those once, and it's definitely not that—but just this immense dread. Because I know I have to sit there for the next hour and just stare at these tiny little cells on the screen. \n\nAnd then, as I'm doing it, I'm constantly second-guessing myself. Like, I'll type in a number, say, 4,500, and my brain will immediately go, 'Wait, was that 4,500 or 5,400?' So I have to look back at the dashboard, verify it, look back at the spreadsheet, and by the time I've done that three times for one single cell, I'm just... I'm so tense. My shoulders are practically up to my ears. I actually had to buy a different desk chair because my neck was hurting so bad from how tense I get. \n\nBut is it stress from the work itself? Not really. I mean, the math isn't hard. It's literally just data transfer. It's the stress of knowing that I'm probably going to mess it up, no matter how hard I try. It's like walking on eggshells in my own brain. And with the checklists, it's the same thing. I'll be going down the line—check, check, check—and I'll start feeling this pressure, like I need to get it done faster, even if there's no real deadline. I just want to be done with it so badly that I end up rushing, and then I get stressed because I know rushing is exactly how I miss a line, but I can't seem to make myself just slow down and look at it calmly. It's just this constant, exhausting tug-of-war in my head the entire time I'm doing these tasks.\n\nDoctor: Are you experiencing any difficulties with memory or attention in your personal relationships?\n\nPatient: Yeah, actually, I do. And it's... it's causing some friction, to be honest, especially at home. It's like I just forget regular life stuff all the time, and it definitely affects my relationships. \n\nLike, with my kids, for example. Just the other week, my youngest needed this specific type of poster board for a school thing. I told him that morning, \"Don't worry buddy, I'll grab it on my way home from work.\" And I had every intention of doing it! I even pictured myself pulling into the store on my commute. But then I leave work, I drive my normal route, I get home, walk through the door, and he's standing there waiting for it... and my stomach just drops because I completely forgot. It just vanished from my brain the second I left the office parking lot. And it's not just a one-time thing, I forget to pick up something I told my kids I'd bring all the time. They get so disappointed, and my wife gets frustrated because she feels like she has to manage everything or else it falls through the cracks.\n\nAnd she's kind of right, because it happens with household stuff, too. Like paying bills. You'd think I'd just set every single thing to autopay, and most things are, but the ones that aren't? I will literally not remember to pay a bill until there's a late notice in the mail. Like our water bill—it comes every quarter, so it's not on my regular monthly radar. I'll listen to it while I'm driving, I'll tell myself, \"Okay, I need to call him back the exact second I park the truck.\" And then I park, grab my bag, walk inside, and I don't think about it again for four days until he emails me asking if I got his message. I just keep dropping the ball on all these everyday things, and it makes the people in my life think I'm ignoring them or that I don't care, which isn't true at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself avoiding your work tasks or putting them off because of the frustration or anxiety they cause you?\n\nPatient: Well, avoid them? Put them off? I mean, I guess I wouldn't say I avoid them entirely, because, well, I can't, right? They're my job. If I don't do the sales reports, my manager is going to be breathing down my neck by Thursday afternoon. But... do I put them off? I don't know if I'd call it putting them off because of anxiety, exactly. It's more like... I'll sit down at my desk on a Tuesday morning, and I know I have to get through this stack of procedural checklists for the new accounts. And I'll look at them, and then I'll think, \"You know what? By then it's almost 10:30, and I'll tell myself, \"Okay, I'll just do it right after lunch, that way I have a solid block of uninterrupted time.\" \n\nSo, am I avoiding it? I don't really think of it as avoiding it in the moment. It feels more like I'm just organizing my day, you know? Prioritizing other things. But then, of course, after lunch rolls around, and I find another reason to push it to 2:00, and then 3:00. And suddenly it's 4:15, and I'm rushing through the checklists just to get them off my desk before I go home, which is exactly when I make those stupid mistakes we talked about earlier. Less sensitive? Or less concerned? Um, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, things bother me *more* than they probably should. I'm definitely not numb to stuff.
